paragraphs: “I really must get to my brother in time today,” Alyosha faltered.
“Of course, of course! You’ve just reminded me. Tell me, what is an aberration?”
“Aberration of what?” Alyosha asked, bewildered.
“In the legal sense. The kind of aberration that excuses everything. Whatever you do, they let you off at once.”
“What are you getting at?”

“I’ll tell you. This Katya ... Ah! She’s a charming, charming creature, but I can never make out who she’s in love with. She was here a while back and I couldn’t get a word out of her. All the more because now she only chats with me about trifles. It’s my health, my health, nothing else, and what a tone she takes with me! So I just said to myself, ‘Well, so be it. I don’t care’... Oh, yes. I was talking about aberration. The doctor has arrived. You know a doctor has arrived? Of course you do—the one who finds out who is mad. You sent for him. No, not you, it was Katya. It’s all Katya’s doing. Now, you see, a man can sit there perfectly sane and all at once have an aberration. He may be fully aware and know what he’s doing, and still be in a state of aberration. And there’s no doubt that Dmitri Fyodorovitch was suffering from aberration. People found out about aberration the moment the law courts were reformed. That is all the good the reformed courts have done. The doctor was here and asked me about that evening, about the gold mines. ‘How did he seem then?’ he asked. He must have been in a state of aberration. He burst in shouting, ‘Money, money, three thousand! Give me three thousand!’ and then he left and did the murder straight away. ‘I don’t want to murder him,’ he said, and suddenly he went and murdered him. That is why they will acquit him: he fought against it, and yet he murdered him.”
“But he didn’t murder him,” Alyosha cut in rather sharply. He was growing sicker and sicker with anxiety and impatience.
“Yes, yes, I know. It was that old man Grigory who murdered him.”
“Grigory?” Alyosha cried.
“Yes, yes, Grigory! He lay where Dmitri Fyodorovitch had knocked him down, then he got up, saw the door standing open, walked in and killed Fyodor Pavlovitch.”
“But why? Why?”

“From aberration. When he came round from the blow Dmitri Fyodorovitch gave him on the head, he was in a state of aberration, and he went and did the murder. As for his saying he didn’t, very likely he just doesn’t remember. Only, you know, it would be better, ever so much better, if it was Dmitri Fyodorovitch who murdered him. And that’s how it must have been, though I keep saying Grigory. It was certainly Dmitri Fyodorovitch, and that’s better, ever so much better! Oh! I don’t mean it’s better that a son should kill his father. I don’t defend that. Children should honor their parents. And yet it would be better if it were he, because then you’d have nothing to weep over, since he did it unconscious—or rather conscious, but without knowing what he was doing. Let them acquit him! That is so humane, and it would show what a blessing the reformed courts are. I knew nothing about all this, but they say the courts have been reformed for a long time. When I heard of it yesterday I was so struck that I wanted to send for you at once. And if he’s acquitted, make him come straight from the courtroom to dine with me. I’ll invite a party of friends and we’ll drink to the reformed courts. I don’t think he’d be dangerous. Besides, I’ll ask a great many friends, so that he could always be led out if he tried anything. And afterwards he could be made a justice of the peace somewhere in another town, since those who have been in trouble themselves make the best judges. And anyway, who isn’t suffering from aberration these days?—you, I, all of us are in a state of aberration, and there are plenty of examples. A man sits singing a song, something suddenly annoys him, he picks up a pistol and shoots the first person he sees, and nobody blames him. I read that recently, and all the doctors confirm it. The doctors are forever confirming; they’ll confirm anything. Why, my Lise is in a state of aberration. She made me cry again yesterday, and the day before, and today I suddenly saw that it’s all aberration. Oh, Lise grieves me so! I think she is completely mad. Why did she send for you? Did she send for you, or did you come of your own accord?”
“She sent for me, and I’m on my way to her now.” Alyosha rose, resolved.

“Oh, my dear, dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, perhaps that’s the most important thing of all,” cried Madame Hohlakov, suddenly bursting into tears. “God knows I entrust Lise to you with all my heart, and I don’t mind that she sends for you on the sly, behind her mother’s back. But forgive me, I can’t so easily entrust my daughter to your brother Ivan Fyodorovitch, though I still take him for the most chivalrous young man. And just imagine, he’s been to see Lise, and I knew nothing about it!”
“What? How? When?” Alyosha was astonished. He had not sat down again but listened on his feet.

“I’ll tell you. Maybe that’s why I asked you here, though now I can’t think why I did. Well, Ivan Fyodorovitch has called on me twice since he came back from Moscow. The first time he came as a friend to pay a visit, and the second time Katya was here, and he came because he’d heard so. I never expected him to come often, of course, knowing how much he has on his hands already, _vous comprenez, cette affaire et la mort terrible de votre papa_. But then I suddenly learned he’d been here once more, not to see me but to see Lise. That was six days ago. He came, stayed five minutes and left. I only heard of it three days later, from Glafira, so it was a great shock. I sent for Lise at once. She laughed. ‘He thought you were asleep,’ she said, ‘and so he came in to ask me how you were.’ Of course, that must be how it was. But Lise, Lise, mercy on us, how she torments me! Would you believe it, one night four days ago, right after you had seen her for the last time and gone, she suddenly had a fit: screaming, shrieking, hysterics! Why do I never have hysterics? Then another fit the next day, and the same on the third, and yesterday too, and then yesterday that aberration. She suddenly yelled, ‘I hate Ivan Fyodorovitch. I insist that you never let him in the house again.’ These astonishing words struck me dumb, and I answered, ‘What grounds could I have for refusing to receive such an excellent young man, and so learned, and so unfortunate, too?’—for all this business is a misfortune, isn’t it? At my words she suddenly burst out laughing, so rudely, you know. Well, I was glad. I thought I’d amused her and the fits would stop, especially since I meant to refuse to receive Ivan Fyodorovitch in any case, because of his strange visits without my knowledge, and to ask him for an explanation. But early this morning Lise woke up and flew into a temper with Yulia and, would you believe it, slapped her face. It’s monstrous. I am always polite to my servants. And an hour later she was clasping Yulia’s feet and kissing them. She sent word that she wasn’t coming to me at all and would never come to see me again, and when I dragged myself down to her, she rushed to kiss me, weeping, and while she kissed me she pushed me out of the room, without a word, so that I couldn’t find out what was wrong. Now, dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, all my hopes rest on you, and of course my whole life is in your hands. I simply beg you to go to Lise and learn everything from her, as only you can, and come back and tell me—me, her mother, for you understand it will be the death of me, simply the death of me, if this goes on, or else I shall run away. I can bear no more. I have patience, but I may lose it, and then ... then something terrible will happen. Ah, dear me! At last, Pyotr Ilyitch!” cried Madame Hohlakov, beaming all over as Perhotin came into the room. “You’re late, you’re late! Well, sit down, speak, relieve our suspense. What does the counsel say? Where are you going, Alexey Fyodorovitch?”
“To see Lise.”
“Oh, yes. You won’t forget what I asked you, will you? It’s a matter of life and death!”
“Of course I won’t forget, if I can ... but I’m so late,” Alyosha muttered, hurrying off.
“No, you must, you must come back. Don’t say ‘If I can.’ I’ll die if you don’t,” Madame Hohlakov called after him, but Alyosha had already left the room.
